items.prompt: What are the two scorecards a decision is made against?
choices: Short-term costs against long-term costs
The written plan against the verbal pitch
Visible merits and the approver's personal stakes
items.explanation: The visible scorecard is the argued case; the invisible one is what the decision means for the approver.

items.prompt: Which item belongs on the visible scorecard?
choices: The projected cost savings of the proposal
The approver's worry about their review
The approver's recent loss of credit
items.explanation: Costs and timelines can be stated openly to the whole room, so they are visible.

items.prompt: Which item belongs on the invisible scorecard?
choices: The migration timeline set out in the plan
How yes would reflect on the approver's own work
The itemized budget attached to the plan
items.explanation: Personal standing is rarely stated aloud, so it stays invisible to outsiders.

items.prompt: In the opening scenario, which scorecard did the original pitch address?
choices: Only the invisible one
Both, but weakly
Only the visible one
items.explanation: The pitch covered cost and merit and never touched what the lead stood to lose.

items.prompt: Who can usually see the invisible scorecard clearly?
choices: The person whose position it describes
Everyone attending the meeting
Whoever wrote the proposal
items.explanation: It lives in one person's position, so outsiders often cannot see it.

items.prompt: A proposal is technically excellent and still rejected. What does that show?
choices: The numbers were secretly wrong
Merit was not the only criterion used
The room did not read it
items.explanation: Being right on the visible scorecard does not guarantee winning the invisible one.

items.prompt: Which word best describes what saying yes or no does to a specific person?
choices: Deadline
Budget
Incentive
items.explanation: An incentive is what makes yes or no feel beneficial or costly to that person.

items.prompt: Who is a stakeholder?
choices: Anyone whose approval or help the proposal needs
Only the most senior person in the room
Only people paid from the project budget
items.explanation: Stakeholders are defined by their influence over the outcome, not by rank or budget.

items.prompt: A neighbour proposes a shared lawn mower for the street. It is technically cheaper for everyone, yet the neighbour who runs a mowing side business says no without discussing price. What is the best reading?
choices: The proposal threatens something on their invisible scorecard
The price comparison must have been miscalculated by the neighbours
They did not understand how sharing equipment actually works
items.explanation: The refusal avoids the numbers entirely, which suggests the deciding factor is personal stakes rather than the visible case.
items.reference:
Two scorecards
👀 Visible: cost, merit, timeline
🫥 Invisible: credit, workload, standing, timing
⚖️ The decision-maker weighs both
Why: a proposal is judged on its merits and on what it means for the person who must approve it.
items.learnMore:
Merit is only half the decision

The visible scorecard is what you can argue in a meeting. The invisible one is what saying yes or no does to the approver personally. A pitch that addresses only the first can win every point and still lose.

Common mistake

Concluding that the proposal was bad because it was rejected. It can be right and still fail the second scorecard.
items.reflection: Think of a time a good suggestion at home, school, or a club was waved off. What might it have meant for the person who said no that you could not see?

items.prompt: Two pitches contain the same facts. One wins, one loses with the same approver. What most likely differs?
choices: The total number of slides used in each one of the pitches
How each pitch connects to what the approver stands to gain or lose
Which pitch happened to have the more accurate numbers in it
items.explanation: Same facts means the visible scorecard is equal; the difference must be in the invisible one.

A better argument would have won had it simply been longer
Best argument on the visible scorecard is not the whole decision

How long will the migration take?
How much money does this save overall?

items.prompt: A well-argued proposal gets a firm 'not right now' with no counter-argument. What is that most likely?
choices: A sign that a hidden factor is deciding
Proof that the proposal was weak
A request for more slides
items.explanation: When nobody disputes the case, the real objection is probably elsewhere.

items.prompt: What is the best first response to an unexplained no?
choices: Repeat the pitch more forcefully
Get curious about what is behind it
Accept it and never raise it again
items.explanation: Curiosity can reveal the hidden constraint; repetition and surrender both skip it.

items.prompt: Which phrase signals that the real objection may be hidden?
choices: 'Your cost figure looks too low'
'Section three contradicts section one'
'Not right now' with no reason given
items.explanation: The other two are specific, checkable objections; a bare 'not now' hides its reason.

items.prompt: If the numbers are not disputed, what should you stop doing?
choices: Strengthening evidence nobody challenged
Asking the approver a few open questions
Reconsidering when the proposal is brought up
items.explanation: More proof for an unchallenged claim does not address the real blocker.

items.prompt: A rejection is best treated as...
choices: An insult to be answered
Information about the decision
A final verdict on the idea
items.explanation: It tells you something about the approver's situation that you can act on.

items.prompt: Which hidden factors might explain an unexplained no?
choices: Only the visual quality of the slides used
Only the length of the meeting it came up in
Timing, credit, workload, or personal risk
items.explanation: These are typical invisible-scorecard items; presentation polish is a visible detail.

items.prompt: What does 'rejection is not an obstacle' mean here?
choices: It carries information you can use next time
You can safely ignore it and move on
It never reflects anything about the proposal
items.explanation: Reading it as data changes your next move.

items.prompt: After an unexplained no, which next step helps most?
choices: Send the same document again
Ask what would make the timing hard for them
Complain to the approver's colleagues
items.explanation: A neutral question can surface the constraint without blame.

items.prompt: A school club votes down a clearly cheaper fundraising plan, and no member objects to the numbers. Which follow-up is most useful?
choices: Re-present the same figures with larger charts
Ask privately what the plan would change for them
Poll the club on whether the figures are right
items.explanation: No one disputed the numbers, so a private question about personal effects is the one likely to find the real blocker.
items.reference:
Reading a no
🚪 No with a counter-argument: debate the argument
🕵️ No without one: look for a hidden factor
🔁 Repeating the pitch does not remove the hidden factor
Why: an unexplained no from a reasonable person usually points at something outside the facts you presented.
items.learnMore:
A no is data

If someone disputes your numbers you can discuss the numbers. If they do not, the objection lives somewhere else: timing, credit, workload, or risk to their standing. Treating it as a puzzle to solve beats treating it as a wall to push on.

Common mistake

Responding to a vague no by sending more evidence for a claim nobody challenged.
items.reflection: Recall a refusal you received that came with no real reason. What factor outside the visible facts could have been behind it?

items.prompt: Which response to an unexplained no treats it as information?
choices: Sending three more supporting reports to them
Waiting a week and then re-sending the same pitch
Asking what makes the moment difficult, then adjusting
items.explanation: Only the first tries to learn what the no reveals before acting.

items.prompt: Was the team lead in the scenario acting in bad faith?
choices: Yes, they deliberately ignored a good idea
No, protecting their team's work was rational for them
Yes, they set out to harm the person proposing
items.explanation: The objection followed from their position, not from ill will.

items.prompt: What does an incentive describe?
choices: How honest a person tends to be generally
How intelligent a person is at their job
What a position rewards and penalises
items.explanation: Incentives are about the situation, not about character.

items.prompt: What does assuming malice do to a diagnosis?
choices: Replaces 'what blocks this?' with 'who is the villain?'
Makes the real blocker easier to locate
Speeds up the path to reaching agreement
items.explanation: A villain story offers no next step, while a blocker can be addressed.

items.prompt: A rational objection can still be...
choices: Impossible for anyone else to understand
Frustrating for the person who proposed
Clear proof that the person acted in bad faith
items.explanation: Understanding the logic of a no does not make it pleasant.

items.prompt: Reading incentives means...
choices: Excusing every refusal you ever receive
Agreeing with every refusal you ever receive
Understanding why the answer makes sense to them
items.explanation: It is about comprehension, not endorsement.

items.prompt: Which is a more useful question than 'why are they so difficult?'
choices: What makes yes costly for them?
How can I show they are wrong?
Who else can overrule them?
items.explanation: The cost question points to something you can address.

items.prompt: A colleague calls the lead 'irrational'. What is the best correction?
choices: They are right; the lead was irrational
The reasoning follows from their position
Rationality is impossible to judge
items.explanation: Rational from their seat is different from agreeing with the result.

items.prompt: Does knowing someone's incentives make you manipulative?
choices: Yes, always
Only if the incentives are financial
No, it is accurate modelling of the situation
items.explanation: The honesty of your case depends on what you do with the understanding, not on having it.

items.prompt: A shopkeeper refuses a neighbourhood plan to share a delivery van, though it would cut costs. Which interpretation fits this unit best?
choices: They simply dislike change and any kind of cooperation
They failed to do the basic cost arithmetic for the van
Sharing may reduce their competitive edge, so refusing is sensible for them
items.explanation: Without evidence of ill will, the more useful reading is that yes would cost them something real.
items.reference:
Incentive is not intent
🧭 Position rewards and punishes
🙂 Rational for them, not villainy
🚫 'Bad faith' ends the diagnosis
Why: people respond sensibly to their situation, so blaming character replaces a useful question with a useless one.
items.learnMore:
Position, not personality

The team lead protected a year of their team's work before a review. That is the same instinct most people would have in their place. Seeing it as rational lets you ask what would make yes safe.

Common mistake

Assuming the person is petty, which closes off the conversation that could have changed the outcome.
items.reflection: Think of someone whose 'no' once annoyed you. What about their position might have made that answer the sensible one for them?

items.prompt: Which inference is a diagnostic error?
choices: 'They rejected it, so they must be acting in bad faith'
'They rejected it, so something may cost them'
'They rejected it, so I should ask what it costs'
items.explanation: Jumping to bad faith ends the inquiry; the other two keep it going.

items.prompt: How many questions does the incentive map ask about each stakeholder?
choices: Two
Seven
Four
items.explanation: Measured on, gains, loses, and timing risk.

items.prompt: The 'measured on' question asks...
choices: What makes this person or team look good
How many years they have worked at the company
How much money they earn in a typical year
items.explanation: It identifies the scoreboard they are judged by.

items.prompt: The 'gains from yes' question asks...
choices: What the company as a whole gets overall
What they personally get if this succeeds
What the person making the proposal gets
items.explanation: The focus is the stakeholder's own benefit.

items.prompt: The 'loses from yes' question asks...
choices: What the proposal costs in dollars to carry out
How long it takes for the approval to arrive
What it could cost them in credit, work or standing
items.explanation: Losses are often invisible to outsiders.

items.prompt: The 'timing risk' question asks...
choices: Why now might be a good or bad moment for them
When the proposal is due to be delivered
How many meetings are left in the quarter
items.explanation: It captures how risk tolerance shifts with circumstances.

items.prompt: Why does timing belong in the map?
choices: Timing never changes what a proposal costs them
The same loss costs more at some moments
It is the easiest of the four to measure
items.explanation: Review season magnifies a loss that would be minor in a quiet month.

items.prompt: Which question is a pitch deck least likely to answer?
choices: What the proposal costs
What the timeline is
What they lose if this succeeds
items.explanation: Decks cover gains and facts; losses to a person are rarely written down.

items.prompt: In the scenario, which answer did most to explain the lead's no?
choices: Their flagship project would look redundant
The migration plan was going to be too slow
The tool being retired was far too expensive
items.explanation: That is the loses-from-yes row.

items.prompt: A colleague's team has just been praised for stability, and you propose a risky rewrite of their system. Which map answer is most likely to predict resistance?
choices: High timing risk, since a failure now would erase fresh credit
Low gains, since rewrites never help anyone in any team
High reward on the visible scorecard for the whole organisation
items.explanation: Recent credit makes any added risk costly right now, which is exactly what the timing question captures.
items.reference:
The four questions
📏 Measured or rewarded on what?
➕ What do they gain if this succeeds?
➖ What do they lose if this succeeds?
⏰ What risk can they tolerate right now?
Why: together the four answers predict a stakeholder's likely position before you pitch.
items.learnMore:
Predicting a position

Each question isolates a different pressure: scoring, upside, downside, and timing. Timing matters because the same loss is cheap at one moment and expensive at another, such as just before a review.

Common mistake

Skipping the timing question, so a pitch that would work in March is delivered in the week it cannot.
items.reflection: Pick someone whose decision you depend on. Which of the four questions do you know the least about, and how could you find out respectfully?

items.prompt: Two stakeholders face the same proposal. One loses nothing; the other loses a project. Which difference explains their opposite reactions?
choices: Their measured-on rows must be identical
The loses-from-yes row differs sharply
Their gains must both be large
items.explanation: The same proposal has different personal consequences for each, so their positions diverge.

items.prompt: What shape does the incentive map take?
choices: A single paragraph of notes
A table with a row per stakeholder
A ranked list of names
items.explanation: One row per stakeholder lets you compare positions.

items.prompt: What should you write in a cell you cannot fill?
choices: A confident guess
Nothing; hide the gap
'Unknown, needs discovery'
items.explanation: Marking ignorance prevents guesses from posing as facts.

items.prompt: Which column is the most useful per the unit?
choices: Loses from yes
Measured on
Name of the stakeholder
items.explanation: Losses are least visible and most predictive.

items.prompt: Why include more than one stakeholder?
choices: It simply makes the finished table look longer
Different people can have opposite incentives
Only the single loudest voice ever matters
items.explanation: A director and a tool owner can read the same proposal very differently.

items.prompt: A good discovery question is...
choices: 'Why are you always being so difficult about this?'
'Do you actually ever read the reports we send?'
'Whose work would this make less visible?'
items.explanation: It seeks real constraints without blaming.

items.prompt: When do you build the map?
choices: Before you pitch
After the pitch is rejected only
Never; it is overkill
items.explanation: Building it in advance lets you shape the pitch.

items.prompt: The map is best treated as...
choices: A guaranteed prediction
A working hypothesis
A secret weapon
items.explanation: It guides questions and gets corrected by conversation.

items.prompt: Who might lose little from yes in the scenario's map?
choices: The tool-owning team lead
The team whose flagship tool retires
The engineering director
items.explanation: The director saves cost without any personal exposure.

items.prompt: A map row reads: 'Measured on: uptime; Gains: none; Loses: pager load rises; Timing: busy launch week.' What does it most directly suggest?
choices: Strong support from this person
That the person is irrelevant to the decision
Resistance, with launch week as the timing amplifier
items.explanation: No gain plus added workload during a pressured week predicts a no.
items.reference:
An incentive map
🗂️ One row per stakeholder
📋 Columns: measured on, gains, loses, timing
❓ Unknown cell: write 'needs discovery'
Why: filling the table honestly before a pitch shows which stakeholder holds the real objection.
items.learnMore:
Using the map honestly

A map is a working hypothesis, not a verdict. Mark what you do not know, then ask respectful discovery questions. Several stakeholders belong on it because the person who rejects is not always the one you expected.

Common mistake

Filling every cell with confident guesses so the map feels complete.

items.explanation: Unknown cells are meant to be turned into knowledge by asking, not by assuming.

items.reference:
An incentive map
🗂️ One row per stakeholder
📋 Columns: measured on, gains, loses, timing
❓ Unknown cell: write 'needs discovery'
Why: filling the table honestly before a pitch shows which stakeholder holds the real objection.
items.learnMore:
Using the map honestly

A map is a working hypothesis, not a verdict. Mark what you do not know, then ask respectful discovery questions. Several stakeholders belong on it because the person who rejects is not always the one you expected.

Common mistake

Filling every cell with confident guesses so the map feels complete.

items.prompt: Which is dishonest framing?

Hiding a real consequence from the approver

items.prompt: A pitch to move a family reunion keeps every fact but names the host aunt as organiser and credits her. Which statement best describes it?

Honest framing, since the facts are unchanged and credit is given truthfully

items.learnMore:
Honest framing

Framing decides which true facts you emphasize and who is credited. It is honest when two people comparing notes would find the same story. It becomes dishonest when it hides a real consequence or claims a benefit that is not there.

Common mistake

Treating 'framing' as a licence to spin; if the other person would feel misled, it has gone too far.

items.prompt: A pitch to merge two clubs was rejected by the older club's president. Which second pitch best follows this unit?
choices: Show a larger savings table than the one shown the first time

items.explanation: It targets the president's loss of standing without altering any facts.
items.reference:
The second pitch
🔢 Numbers: unchanged
🧱 Plan and timeline: unchanged
🏷️ Changed: who leads, and whose win it is
Why: it aims at the loses-from-yes row by giving the threatened team a truthful new story about the same work.
items.learnMore:
Same facts, new owner

The second pitch kept the plan, savings and architecture identical. It replaced 'we are fixing your tool' with 'your team leads this, using what only it knows'. That is a different story about the same facts, and it removes the thing the lead stood to lose.

Common mistake

Believing a second pitch must contain new evidence; here the facts were never the problem.

items.prompt: Does one technique fix every rejection?
choices: Yes, reframing always works
Yes, waiting always works
No, it depends on the blocking row
items.explanation: Different rows need different levers.

items.prompt: What does 'cost of saying no' mean?
choices: Making the downside of rejecting visible
Charging the approver a fee for delaying
Refusing to negotiate until they agree
items.explanation: If no also has a cost, the calculus shifts.

items.prompt: What is a 'lower-visibility first step'?
choices: Hiding the plan from everyone who might object
A smaller trial that avoids a public declaration
Doing the whole piece of work in secret
items.explanation: A small trial tests the idea without staging someone's embarrassment.

items.prompt: If the same team's projects keep being targeted, the issue is...
choices: A single badly designed slide in one deck
A wrong number somewhere in the budget table
A pattern bigger than one pitch
items.explanation: Repeated outcomes call for a broader conversation.

items.prompt: Is the incentive map useless when timing and framing are blocked?
choices: No, it still diagnoses which lever remains
Yes, it should be dropped at that point
Yes, it only ever works when timing can move
items.explanation: The map shows that the remaining levers are cost of no or a smaller step.

items.prompt: Which is a failure mode listed in the unit?
choices: Asking respectful questions to find out more
Making the technical case stronger after a rejection
Mapping several stakeholders before the first pitch
items.explanation: A stronger case ignores the real blocker.

items.prompt: Which is another failure mode?
choices: Changing the pitch once the incentive is understood
Writing down the cells that are still unknown
Identifying the incentive but not changing the pitch
items.explanation: Understanding is only diagnostic; the next pitch has to change.

items.prompt: Which other units fit the 'pattern' problem?
choices: The corporate-politics units on influence and power
The unit on writing clear status emails
The unit on building spreadsheets for budgets
items.explanation: Who keeps absorbing costs is a power question.

items.prompt: Reframing ownership is impossible and the deadline is fixed. Which move best fits this unit?
choices: Show that rejecting also has a concrete cost
Repeat the first pitch more slowly
Wait quietly until the deadline passes
items.explanation: With both usual levers closed, cost of no or a smaller step remains.
items.reference:
Match fix to blocker
🧭 Loses blocking: reframe ownership
⏳ Timing blocking: wait or phase it
🧾 Neither can move: show cost of no, or start small
🔁 Same team, again: pattern problem
Why: no single technique works regardless of which row is blocking.
items.learnMore:
No universal fix

The reframing worked because ownership could move. When it cannot, the map points to making the cost of saying no visible, or to a smaller first step that avoids a public 'your work was redundant' moment. A repeated pattern is a different, larger conversation.

Common mistake

Applying the last technique that worked without checking which row is blocking this time.
